Steady: Methodical and dependable. Shows up, ships code, and never creates drama.
Quiet contributor who delivers consistently, quarter after quarter.
Not flashy, but never a bottleneck. Teammates rely on them without thinking about it.
Prefers a clear backlog and a good pair of headphones. Gets things done.
The kind of engineer who makes the on-call rotation less stressful just by being on it.
Consistent output, low maintenance. Exactly what a growing team needs.
Measured, reliable, and genuinely okay with unglamorous work.
Solid baseline performer. Never skips the boring parts of the job.
Zero drama, high delivery. Rarely the loudest voice, but often the most useful.
Has strong opinions, loosely held. Anchoring when needed, adaptable when not.
Shows up every day and does what needs doing. Underrated quality at every stage.
Rarely the first to speak in a meeting, but always the first to deliver.
Ambitious: Wants to own a roadmap by Q3. Brings serious energy when morale is solid.
The first to volunteer for high-stakes projects. Watch out when they're under-challenged.
Excellent when pointed at a hard problem. Needs a clear growth path or they'll find one elsewhere.
Driven by impact metrics, not just shipping velocity. Results-oriented to a fault.
Has a 5-year plan that includes your company's valuation doubling. Sometimes that's a good thing.
Thrives in pressure. Finds coasting more uncomfortable than crunch.
Ambitious without being cutthroat. Lifts the bar for everyone on the team.
High ceiling, high expectations. Give them a hard problem and get out of the way.
Moves fast, learns from failures, then moves faster. Has strong opinions on what good looks like.
Will join to grow. Will leave if growth stalls. Keep them challenged.
Treats every quarter as a new opportunity to outperform the last one.
Has already mapped out what their next title should be. Could be a good thing.
Perfectionist: Finds the bug everyone else missed. Slightly slower than you'd like on green-field features.
The person who actually reads the RFC before building. Pays off in the long run.
Catches edge cases in code review that would have cost you users. Indispensable on quality-sensitive work.
Slower to ship features, but rarely ships problems. Great on reliability-critical paths.
Cannot let known technical debt exist without flagging it. A blessing and occasionally a bottleneck.
Holds the team to a high bar. Sometimes painfully so. Worth it.
Has opinions about error handling, logging, and observability. Surprisingly correct opinions.
Prefers to do it right over doing it fast. Good for systems that will matter in two years.
Will rewrite a function three times before they're satisfied. The third version is usually excellent.
The kind of engineer who writes the test first and means it.
Keeps tech debt honest. Will not pretend the workaround is a real fix.
Documentation is not an afterthought for them. The rest of the team thanks them later.
Team Player: Makes every sprint slightly better just by being in it. Easy collaborator, natural unblocked.
Dependable across assignments and a genuine team-first attitude. Retention asset.
Not the highest individual output on paper, but the team performs better when they're around.
First to help unblock a stuck teammate. Reduces friction across the org.
Collaborative by nature, not policy. Great for teams that are scaling fast.
The glue between subteams. Reduces misalignment without being told to.
Balanced contributor. Never hoards context, always shares findings.
Builds cross-functional relationships naturally. Teams run smoother with them involved.
Great at translating between technical and non-technical stakeholders. Quietly valuable.
Puts the team's velocity before their own headline metrics. A genuine asset.
Keeps the team healthy when pressure builds. That's harder than it looks.
Invests in shared tooling and documentation others actually use. Rare.
Mentor: Makes junior teammates better. Their influence compounds over time.
Experienced enough to have war stories, patient enough to share them constructively.
Slows their own output to bring up the people around them. Worth it at scale.
Has onboarded more junior engineers than they can count. Most of them flourished.
Invests in others' growth. The kind of person who makes your whole team stronger.
Not chasing seniority metrics. Genuinely cares about the people they work with.
Code reviews are thorough and educational, not ego-driven. Rare and valuable.
Will spend 20 minutes explaining a concept so a junior doesn't spend 4 hours confused.
Team multiplier. Individual output is good; team output is great when they're involved.
Institutional knowledge made human. Preserves context that would otherwise walk out the door.
Develops teammates the way a good coach develops players. Consistently.
The reason some of your best engineers didn't quit in their first year.
Adaptable: Comfortable wearing different hats. Effective across more role types than their title suggests.
One of the fastest learners on any team they join. Picks up new stacks quickly.
Does not need a rigid job description. Fills gaps wherever the team needs it.
Moved across three different tech stacks in two years. Performed well in all of them.
Responds well to ambiguity. Good for early-stage environments where the scope shifts constantly.
Will pivot from feature work to incident response without losing composure.
Effective across Frontend, Backend, and DevOps depending on what the quarter demands.
Low resistance to change. Gets productive in new environments faster than almost anyone.
Thrives in companies that are still figuring out who does what. Great for your stage.
Good at figuring out what needs to be done without being told. Especially useful pre-PMF.
Doesn't mind when the plan changes. Usually the one who helps make the new plan.
Works well in ambiguity, executes well under clarity. Can handle both.

Junior: Early in their career, but eager.
Still finding their footing, but promising.
Mid: A couple of years in, growing fast.
Senior: Been around long enough to know what matters.
Lead: Has led projects from scoping to ship.
Balances technical depth with team ownership.
Principal: Sets technical direction across the org.
Operates at the intersection of strategy and code.
